title: Role of Responsive Neurostimulation in Managing Drug-Resistant Epilepsy: A Systematic Review of Clinical Outcomes
clinical_background: Drug-resistant epilepsy involves persistent seizures despite treatment with multiple antiepileptic drugs, and conventional approaches are inadequate for a substantial subset of patients. RNS detects abnormal brain electrical activity and delivers stimulation before seizure symptoms emerge. Its increasing clinical use has produced evidence on effectiveness and safety, but variation in patient outcomes makes a synthesis of that evidence necessary.
objectives: Critically assess and synthesize clinical outcomes associated with RNS in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy.
Evaluate seizure reduction, quality of life, and the prevalence of adverse effects associated with RNS.
Identify patterns in treatment responsiveness and discuss implications for clinical practice and future research.
study_design: Systematic review conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Medline, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Scopus were searched from each database’s inception through April 2024. Reference lists were checked, and clinical trial registries and relevant conference proceedings were searched to identify additional research. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data; a third reviewer helped resolve eligibility disagreements.

population.description: Individuals with drug-resistant epilepsy evaluated for clinical outcomes after RNS.
inclusion_criteria: English-language, peer-reviewed studies published through April 2024.
Clinical trials, randomized controlled trials, observational or cohort studies, case series, and meta-analyses examining RNS efficacy and safety in drug-resistant epilepsy.
Studies reporting outcomes relevant to seizure reduction, responder rates, quality of life, or safety.
exclusion_criteria: Studies that did not examine RNS or its direct effects in drug-resistant epilepsy.
Non-peer-reviewed publications and grey literature, including conference abstracts and unpublished work.
Studies published in languages other than English.
Studies without sufficiently detailed outcomes or methodological descriptions to assess intervention effects.

primary: Safety, including adverse effects and complications

statistical_methods: The authors used a qualitative, narrative synthesis rather than a meta-analysis because study designs and patient demographics varied. Findings were organized by seizure reduction, responder rates, adverse events, and quality of life.
quality_assessment_tool: AMSTAR 2 for systematic reviews and meta-analyses; ROBINS-I for non-randomized studies; and the Cochrane Collaboration’s Risk of Bias tool for randomized controlled trials.
interpretation: The authors interpret the evidence as supporting RNS as an effective option for drug-resistant epilepsy, with reduced seizure frequency, improved quality of life and a favorable safety profile. They note that reductions in seizure frequency reached up to 75% in the studies discussed. In Meador et al. [10], 44% of participants reported meaningful quality-of-life improvement. Variation in outcomes may reflect differences in patient selection, electrode placement and stimulation settings. The authors also suggest that age and seizure-onset location may influence response. They describe interruption of seizure propagation and longer-term changes in neural networks as possible, rather than established, explanations for the effect.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The review is consistent with earlier evidence of seizure reduction, including the findings of Kusyk et al. [7]. The authors consider its synthesis across different patient groups to reinforce that evidence and to draw greater attention to quality-of-life outcomes beyond seizure control.
clinical_implications: RNS may offer a treatment option for people with drug-resistant epilepsy who have not responded to pharmacotherapy or are unsuitable for invasive surgery.
Differences in response across patients suggest that individual characteristics and seizure profiles may matter when anticipating benefit.
Better seizure control could reduce hospitalizations and emergency visits and potentially offset substantial initial costs, although the authors present this as a possibility.
The procedure’s invasiveness and the demands of device management may affect adherence and satisfaction despite improvements in seizures and quality of life.
practice_implications: The authors recommend incorporating RNS into standard epilepsy treatment protocols as an option for appropriate patients.
They call for careful patient selection, precise implantation and individualized stimulation settings, supported by specialized training for clinical teams.
They suggest that treatment plans account for patient preferences and circumstances, with education about RNS benefits and challenges and continuing support.
They suggest that treatment guidelines may need updating to reflect neuromodulation and that coverage and reimbursement policies may need adjustment to improve access.
limitations: Small samples and short follow-up in included studies may limit generalizability and leave long-term outcomes or late complications insufficiently characterized.
Potential selection bias and the absence of control groups in some studies may favor RNS.
Patient selection criteria, electrode placement and stimulation settings were not reported consistently across studies, complicating interpretation of differences in outcomes.
strengths: The authors identify the comprehensive search and rigorous synthesis of evidence from varied study designs and patient populations as strengths of the review.
open_questions: How RNS compares directly with other neuromodulation therapies in efficacy and safety remains unresolved.
The durability of seizure and quality-of-life improvements, and the possibility of late adverse effects, require clarification.
The patient characteristics, epilepsy etiologies, implantation approaches and stimulation settings that best predict benefit remain uncertain.
Whether adaptive RNS systems could improve outcomes as seizure patterns change remains to be investigated.
future_directions: Conduct more RCTs directly comparing RNS with vagus nerve stimulation or deep brain stimulation.
Study long-term seizure control, quality of life and late-emerging adverse effects.
Investigate outcomes in specific groups, including pediatric patients and people with different epilepsy etiologies, to refine patient selection.
Standardize reporting of selection criteria, electrode placement and stimulation parameters.
Explore personalized and adaptive RNS approaches, including systems that adjust to changing seizure patterns.

notable_adverse_events: Touma et al., 2022 attributed hoarseness, cough, and throat pain to VNS; rates were not specified.
Touma et al., 2022 attributed implant-site pain, headache, and dysesthesia to RNS/DBS; rates were not specified.
Kusyk et al., 2022 reported an 18.9% complication rate with RNS, including device-related infections; an infection-specific rate was not given.
Kerezoudis et al., 2022 reported an 8% complication rate in pediatric RNS recipients, including four infections, and reported no major deficits.
Levy et al., 2023 reported an 8.4% complication rate in pediatric RNS recipients; half of the complications were device-related infections.

subgroup_analyses: Kerezoudis et al., 2022 reported that the pediatric RNS responder proportion varied by epilepsy type, without providing type-specific estimates.
Meador et al., 2015 observed QOL improvement regardless of seizure origin; origin-specific estimates were not provided.
secondary_results: The review identified 133 records, removed nine duplicates, screened 124 records, selected 58 for more detailed evaluation, examined 44 reports for eligibility, and included five studies.
Touma et al., 2022 reported that seizure freedom increased over time for DBS and RNS, without providing rates.
Kusyk et al., 2022 reported a mean responder rate of 68% (95% CI: 60%-75%) using a threshold of >50% seizure reduction.
Kerezoudis et al., 2022 reported that 80% of pediatric RNS recipients were responders.
Levy et al., 2023 reported that 57% of pediatric RNS recipients achieved Engel Class <2 and that 9.7% achieved seizure freedom.
Meador et al., 2015 reported that 16% of participants had a decline in QOL at 2 years and found no adverse mood changes.

main_conclusion: The authors conclude that RNS meaningfully reduces seizures and improves quality of life in drug-resistant epilepsy while retaining a favorable safety profile. They advocate broader inclusion of RNS in epilepsy care, with treatment tailored to individual patients and attention to selection, procedural, and cost-related challenges.
narrative_summary:
This systematic review examined clinical outcomes of RNS for drug-resistant epilepsy. Following PRISMA guidance, the authors searched PubMed, Medline, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Scopus through April 2024 and included five studies. Because study designs and patient populations differed, they synthesized the findings qualitatively rather than conducting a new meta-analysis. The included evidence comprised reviews, meta-analyses, and an RCT.

In the included Kusyk et al. analysis, mean seizure reduction was 68% (95% CI: 61%-76%), and the mean responder rate was 68% (95% CI: 60%-75%). The pediatric studies reported a median reduction of 75% (IQR: 50-88%) in Kerezoudis et al. and a median reduction of 75% at 12 months in Levy et al. In the Meador et al. trial, 44% reported improved QOL at 2 years, whereas 16% reported a decline; adverse mood changes were not reported. The authors interpret the overall evidence as supporting RNS for patients with drug-resistant epilepsy, including those unsuitable for invasive surgery.

Interpretation remains constrained by small samples, short follow-up, possible selection bias, and absent control groups in some studies. The authors call for longer-term research, direct comparisons with other neuromodulation therapies, and improved patient selection and treatment customization.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Drug-resistant epilepsy remains difficult to manage when conventional antiepileptic drugs fail. Responsive neurostimulation (RNS) is a potential treatment, but broad syntheses of its clinical outcomes have been limited. This systematic review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidance and searched PubMed, Medline, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Scopus for literature through April 2024. It examined peer-reviewed evidence on RNS efficacy, safety, and quality of life in drug-resistant epilepsy, including clinical trials, cohort studies, and meta-analyses while excluding irrelevant and non-peer-reviewed work. Five studies met the criteria. Across them, RNS was associated with significant seizure-frequency reductions, better quality of life, and a favorable safety profile. Small samples and possible selection bias limit the evidence, although benefits appeared consistent across varied patient groups. The authors consider RNS a viable, effective option and recommend incorporating it into standard epilepsy management protocols. They call for research on long-term outcomes and improved patient selection.

document_sections.heading: Introduction And Background
document_sections.content: Drug-resistant epilepsy involves seizures that persist despite multiple antiepileptic drugs, and established treatments do not adequately help a substantial proportion of patients. RNS uses a closed-loop system to identify abnormal brain electrical activity and deliver pulses intended to normalize it before seizure symptoms develop. Its intended benefits include fewer seizures and better quality of life, with fewer adverse effects than approaches such as resective surgery or chronic medication. Growing clinical use and technological progress have produced more efficacy and safety evidence, but changing technology and varied patient outcomes make synthesis necessary to clarify benefits, limitations, and research gaps. The review aims to assess RNS-associated seizure reduction, quality of life, and adverse effects; identify response patterns; and consider implications for clinical decisions and future research.

document_sections.heading: Search Strategy
document_sections.content: The authors designed their search around PRISMA guidance and searched PubMed, Medline, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Scopus from each database’s inception through April 2024. They combined relevant keywords and MeSH terms concerning epilepsy, drug-resistant or refractory epilepsy, neurostimulation, responsive neurostimulation, and RNS with AND and OR operators. They also checked selected articles’ reference lists, clinical trial registries, and neurological and neurosurgical conference proceedings for additional, unpublished, or ongoing research. The search was restricted to English-language studies in peer-reviewed journals and sought clinical trials, cohort studies, case series, and meta-analyses reporting clinical RNS outcomes in drug-resistant epilepsy.

document_sections.heading: Eligibility Criteria
document_sections.content: Eligible peer-reviewed English-language articles investigated RNS efficacy and safety in diagnosed drug-resistant epilepsy. Permitted designs included clinical trials, randomized controlled trials (RCTs), observational and cohort studies, and meta-analyses, published from database inception through April 2024. Outcomes of interest were seizure-frequency reduction, responder rates, quality of life, and safety. The authors excluded studies unrelated to RNS effects in this population, non-peer-reviewed work, conference abstracts and other grey literature, unpublished work, non-English publications, and studies without sufficiently complete outcome data or clear methods to assess intervention effects.

document_sections.heading: Data Extraction
document_sections.content: Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, classifying articles by relevance. Potentially eligible articles then underwent full-text assessment using a purpose-built Microsoft Excel form completed independently by each reviewer against the predefined criteria. When eligibility was disputed or unclear, a third reviewer participated in discussion to reach consensus. Extracted information covered lead author, publication year, design, sample size, primary RNS efficacy and safety outcomes, secondary outcomes, and reported limitations or biases.

document_sections.heading: Data Analysis and Synthesis
document_sections.content: Because study designs and patient demographics varied, the authors used qualitative rather than meta-analytic synthesis. They compared evidence on efficacy, safety, and quality of life, organizing findings around seizure reduction, responder rates, and adverse events. The narrative synthesis also examined shared patterns, differences, research gaps, and possible directions for improving RNS treatment.

document_sections.heading: Study Selection Process
document_sections.content: The searches produced 133 records. After nine duplicates were removed, 124 records were screened; 58 were chosen for more detailed evaluation. Eligibility assessment then examined 44 reports closely, and five new studies were included. A PRISMA flowchart presents this selection process.

document_sections.heading: Characteristics of Selected Studies
document_sections.content: The review included five studies conducted between 2015 and 2023, comprising RCTs, observational work, and meta-analyses. Together they addressed seizure reduction, safety, quality of life, pediatric populations, longer-term outcomes, and RNS complications. The authors identify small samples, short follow-up, and potential study-selection bias as recurring limitations. Table 1 summarizes each study’s objective, methods, outcomes, complications, and interpretation. The five studies underwent design-appropriate quality assessment: AMSTAR 2 for systematic reviews and meta-analyses, ROBINS-I for non-randomized studies, and the Cochrane Collaboration’s Risk of Bias tool for RCTs. These assessments considered matters including search and selection methods, confounding, participant selection, random sequence generation, and blinding. Table 2 compares the studies’ methodological strengths and limitations.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content:
The authors interpret the combined evidence as supporting RNS for drug-resistant epilepsy. They cite Kusyk et al. and Levy et al. for substantial seizure-frequency reductions and responder outcomes, including median reductions of up to 75%. They cite Meador et al. for meaningful quality-of-life improvement in 44% of participants after RNS. Reported complication rates in pediatric and adult populations were relatively low, supporting a favorable safety assessment. The findings agree with earlier evidence on seizure reduction while emphasizing quality-of-life benefits beyond seizure control. Variation in seizure and quality-of-life outcomes may reflect patient selection, electrode placement, and stimulation parameters, which studies did not report consistently. The authors therefore call for standardized reporting. They suggest that age and epilepsy-onset location, particularly younger age and neocortical onset, may relate to different responses and warrant more individualized treatment.

RNS detects abnormal electrical activity and delivers targeted stimulation before seizures manifest. The authors describe interruption of seizure spread and increased local inhibition as likely mechanisms, and consider longer-term changes in neural plasticity possible rather than established. They propose RNS as an option within current protocols for patients who do not respond to pharmacotherapy or are unsuitable for invasive surgery. Effective implementation requires careful selection, precise implantation, individualized stimulation settings, and specialized clinical-team training.

The included evidence is limited by small samples, short follow-up that may miss durable outcomes or late complications, possible selection bias, and absent control groups in some studies that could favor RNS. The authors regard their broad search and systematic analysis across varied designs and populations as strengths. They call for more RCTs directly comparing RNS with vagus nerve stimulation or deep brain stimulation, longer-term studies of seizure control, quality of life, and late adverse effects, and research in pediatric and other etiologically distinct subgroups. They also propose studying treatment tailored to individual seizure profiles and adaptive systems that respond to changing patterns; artificial intelligence-driven neurostimulation remains a future possibility.

The authors suggest that including RNS in standard care could require guideline, coverage, and reimbursement changes. Although initial costs are substantial, fewer hospitalizations and emergency visits might produce longer-term savings. They note that procedural invasiveness and device management can affect adherence and satisfaction despite benefits for many patients. Understanding patient preferences, providing education about benefits and difficulties, and maintaining support may improve acceptance and sustained use.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: The authors conclude that the reviewed evidence supports a significant therapeutic benefit of RNS in drug-resistant epilepsy, with fewer seizures, improved quality of life, and a favorable safety profile. They view it as a viable alternative for people who have exhausted other options. They emphasize tailoring treatment to individual characteristics and improving patient selection and RNS application. Cost and procedural challenges remain. The authors advocate broader inclusion of RNS in epilepsy protocols and greater healthcare-system access, while presenting its incorporation into standard care as a potential change in epilepsy management.
